title: Proposed emergency earthquake fund will help prepare for catastrophe, insurance industry says
html:
A damaged road is inspected by municipal officials in southern Japan, on July 31. Many Canadians face significant earthquake risk, particularly in southwestern British Columbia and the region between Ottawa and Quebec City.Taichi Nagahisa/The Canadian Press

After decades of raising the alarm, Canada’s insurance industry says the federal government’s proposal to create a $50-billion emergency earthquake fund will help prepare for catastrophic events that could hit B.C and Quebec within the next 50 years.

As part of the recent federal budget, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced the government’s intention to introduce legislation that would create the Canadian Earthquake Insurance Facility, an emergency backstop that would provide up to $50-billion to the property and casualty insurance sector following an extreme earthquake.

There were several other new natural disaster preparedness initiatives that Mr. Champagne announced, which included strengthening wildfire protection in First Nations communities and boosting funding for waterbombers used to fight wildfires.

Experts have long warned that a catastrophic earthquake could cause unprecedented damage to homes, businesses and infrastructure, with significant economic ramifications across the country for years following an event.

For decades, property and casualty insurers have called for a government response on earthquake risk, saying Canada is the only G7 country with significant seismic risk that doesn’t have a solution in place. A major earthquake would not only create solvency challenges for some insurance companies, but it would also have an effect on the mortgage and banking sectors.

The proposed $50-billion earthquake fund would alleviate that pressure and would be financed through nominal levies on insurers. The fund would help support victims by increasing insurers’ ability to pay claims and promote financial stability, the government said in the budget.

“Earthquakes are not events that we should see as unforeseeable. We know they represent a risk to housing availability and affordability, and obviously a risk to the insurance system,” Lisa Guglietti, executive vice-president of property and casualty at The Co-operators Group Ltd., the insurance co-operative, said in an interview.

Ms. Guglietti says she is encouraged by the government’s proposal to set up a facility that is funded by the industry, ensuring costs are not transferred onto taxpayers.

“We believe that insurers and reinsurers really should continue to bear significant amount of the earthquake risk, but there is this kind of extreme tail or black swan events that can occur and when that happens, the consequences go beyond what individual insurers or the system can support.”

Canada is also the only G7 country with significant earthquake risk that lacks a public-private partnership under which the government would take on some amount of liability for damages.

The bulk of earthquakes are manageable for major insurers, Ms. Guglietti said, including events that may cause up to $35-billion in damage.

“When you get to about $35-billion to $45-billion ranges, you’re going to have a couple insurance companies that can’t make it, and then when you get to $45-billion plus, it’s widespread contagion,” she added.

In a report released last year, the Insurance Bureau of Canada (IBC) estimates a 9.0-magnitude earthquake would result in total economic losses of $128-billion and 43,700 jobs over the subsequent 10 years.

Insured losses could cost the insurance industry about $52.6-billion, more than 11 times the Fort McMurray wildfire in 2016, which cost insurers $4.7-billion in losses.

Intact Financial executive Darren Godfrey says the company has been advocating to the government for more than 20 years for a national earthquake framework, and “applauds” Ottawa for proactively planning to put facilities in place.

“Now, we have a mechanism that we can activate quickly during a time of need,” Mr. Godfrey said in an interview. “Canada is extremely well-placed in terms of the way we manage earthquake today, but this is just another layer of support, so when the time comes - and it will at some point unfortunately - the government doesn’t need to worry about how we rebuild the insurance industry.”

Many Canadians face significant earthquake risk, particularly in southwestern British Columbia and the region between Ottawa and Quebec City. There is an average of 4,000 earthquakes in Canada every year, although most are minor events that go unnoticed. However, there are areas in the country that sit on fault lines, which could produce an earthquake with a magnitude of 7.0 or greater.

The highest-risk zones are the Pacific Coast, known as the Cascadia Subduction Zone, one of the most volatile fault lines in the world, with scientists estimating a 30-per-cent chance of a magnitude 8 or greater earthquake within the next 50 years.

Victor Adesanya, senior vice-president of global insurance at Morningstar DBRS, said in a report last week that a catastrophic earthquake could rapidly deplete insurers’ capital and trigger negative rating actions.

“The facility should reduce the risk of multiple insurer failures and protect regulatory capital,” he said. “A federal backstop would limit extreme loss exposure, improve financial resilience, and reduce the potential for one insurer’s failure to affect the entire sector.”

The IBC says that while Canada’s property and casualty insurance sector is among the best prepared in the world for earthquake losses, the most extreme earthquakes can place extraordinary pressure on the insurance system, affecting its ability to respond and continue essential insurance services.

“A major earthquake is a question of when, not if,” Celyeste Power, IBC’s president and chief executive officer said in a statement following the budget. “By establishing the Canadian Earthquake Insurance Facility to help manage the financial consequences of a catastrophic earthquake, the federal government is taking meaningful action to address a well-understood systemic risk and reduce the potential burden on taxpayers and impact on insurance consumers.”

The legislation would be reviewed five years after implementation to assess its impact on the earthquake insurance market, and the government would work with provinces and territories to extend access to provincially regulated insurers.
summary: Experts have long warned a devastating quake could cause unprecedented damage to homes, businesses and infrastructure
